questions.statement: Read the paragraph: Our school recycles paper and plastic every Friday. Students sort waste into special bins. Teachers explain why recycling protects nature. What is the main idea?
questions.context: Lucia is practising reading skills for her English exam in class.

options.text: School recycling every Friday is the central point of the paragraph.
options.feedback: Correct! School recycling every Friday is the central point because every sentence explains how students organise that weekly activity.

options.text: The paragraph is mainly about the colour of the blue bins.
options.feedback: The sentence about blue bins is wrong because it mentions only one detail about containers and ignores the wider weekly recycling programme.

options.text: The paragraph is mainly about a history teacher with old maps.
options.feedback: The sentence about the history teacher is wrong because it picks a small example from one lesson and misses the main recycling message.

options.text: The paragraph is mainly about a school trip to Madrid.
options.feedback: The sentence about a trip to Madrid is wrong because no trip appears in the paragraph and it cannot represent the recycling idea.

questions.explanation: The main idea is the central point the whole paragraph supports. Details and examples prove it but cannot replace it when you summarise.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the advert: Join our team today! Football is fun, healthy and for everyone. Sign up this week! What is the purpose of the text?
questions.context: Marco is learning to recognise the purpose of short English texts.

options.text: To persuade students to join the sports club this term.
options.feedback: Correct! Joining the sports club is a persuasion text because Join our team today directly invites the reader to take action now.

options.text: To inform readers about new library opening hours.
options.feedback: The option about informing library hours is wrong because the text never gives opening times and instead urges the reader to join.

options.text: To entertain readers with a funny story about training.
options.feedback: The option about telling a funny story is wrong because there is no humour or story, only direct encouragement to participate.

options.text: To explain how to do a science experiment step by step.
options.feedback: The option about explaining an experiment is wrong because no scientific process is described and no steps or results are presented.

questions.explanation: Authors write to inform, persuade, entertain or explain. Persuasive texts use calls to action and positive adjectives to change behaviour.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the paragraph: Mobile phones must be silent in class. Students can check messages at break. Teachers keep the rules fair. Which sentence states the main idea?
questions.context: Sara is training to separate main ideas from supporting details.

options.text: Students should use phones responsibly during lessons.
options.feedback: Correct! Responsible phone use in class is the main idea because rules about silent mode and break time all support that general point.

options.text: Students may use phones only during the morning break.
options.feedback: The sentence about break time only is wrong because using phones at break is just one detail that supports the wider rule about responsible use.

options.text: A new phone brand is the best choice for students.
options.feedback: The sentence about a new phone brand is wrong because the paragraph never advertises a brand and focuses on classroom behaviour instead.

options.text: All phones should be banned from schools forever.
options.feedback: The sentence about banning all phones forever is wrong because the text allows limited use and never proposes a total permanent ban.

questions.explanation: Supporting details give examples or reasons for the main idea. A single break time or brand name is too narrow to be the whole message.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Paragraph: Cycling to school saves money and keeps you fit. It avoids traffic jams. It also reduces pollution. Which sentence is the topic sentence?
questions.context: Pablo is identifying topic sentences in short English paragraphs.

options.text: Cycling to school saves money and keeps you fit.
options.feedback: Correct! Cycling to school saves money and keeps you fit is the topic sentence because it introduces the general benefit developed by later details.

options.text: On rainy days some students prefer taking the bus.
options.feedback: The sentence about rainy days and the bus is wrong because it gives only one weather exception instead of introducing the whole cycling topic.

options.text: Maria bought a strong new lock for her bicycle.
options.feedback: The sentence about Marias new lock is wrong because it reports a small personal detail that cannot introduce the general paragraph.

options.text: You need a pump to repair a flat tyre quickly.
options.feedback: The sentence about repairing a flat tyre is wrong because it describes one maintenance detail and does not cover the wider benefits of cycling.

questions.explanation: The topic sentence often opens a paragraph and states the main idea. Later sentences add details, so the first general sentence is the best guide.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the story: We lost our suitcase, Dad wore beach sandals to dinner, and we laughed all night. What is the purpose of this story?
questions.context: Elena is studying how to detect texts written to entertain.

options.text: To entertain readers with a funny holiday story.
options.feedback: Correct! To entertain with a funny holiday story is right because the lost suitcase and beach sandals create humour rather than factual instruction.

options.text: To inform readers about new train times and prices.
options.feedback: The option about informing of train times is wrong because the story gives no schedules or prices and centres on amusing holiday events.

options.text: To persuade readers to buy a brand of sun cream.
options.feedback: The option about persuading to buy sun cream is wrong because no product is promoted and no purchase call appears in the narrative.

options.text: To explain the rules for completing homework correctly.
options.feedback: The option about explaining homework rules is wrong because no school rules are described and the tone is playful instead of instructional.

questions.explanation: Texts written to entertain use humour, adventure and surprising events. They focus on enjoyment rather than giving instructions or factual data.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Notice: The school library opens from nine to six from Monday to Friday. Books can be borrowed for two weeks. What is the purpose?
questions.context: Diego is learning to spot purely informative news texts.

options.text: To inform readers about new library opening hours.
options.feedback: Correct! To inform about library hours is right because the notice gives factual opening times in neutral language without persuasion.

options.text: To persuade readers to join a local gym this month.
options.feedback: The option about persuading to join a gym is wrong because the notice mentions no sport and contains no call to join anything.

options.text: To entertain readers with jokes about books and exams.
options.feedback: The option about entertaining with jokes is wrong because the notice has no humour and only presents practical factual information.

options.text: To describe an exciting football match last weekend.
options.feedback: The option about describing a football match is wrong because no game or score is reported and the focus is library service hours.

questions.explanation: Informative texts present facts such as dates, places and times in neutral language. They do not sell products or tell jokes as their main goal.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Advert: Fresh fruit market! Apples, oranges and bananas at low prices. Open every Saturday near the park. What is the main idea?
questions.context: Carmen is practising main idea questions with short adverts.

options.text: A local market sells fresh and affordable fruit.
options.feedback: Correct! A local market sells fresh and affordable fruit is the main idea because every line promotes that central benefit for families.

options.text: Apples at the market cost exactly two euros.
options.feedback: The sentence about apples costing two euros is wrong because the price is only one supporting detail and not the whole market message.

options.text: The market has a large car park for visitors.
options.feedback: The sentence about a market car park is wrong because parking is a minor facility detail and misses the fresh food focus.

options.text: Someone lost a wallet near the market entrance.
options.feedback: The sentence about a lost wallet is wrong because no lost property is mentioned and it is unrelated to the advert purpose.

questions.explanation: The main idea of an advert combines product and benefit. Price details alone are supporting facts that help sell the central healthy eating message.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Poster: Vote for a cleaner school! Bring your bottle, save water, plant a tree. Act now! What is the purpose?
questions.context: Lucia is studying persuasive techniques in school campaign texts.

options.text: To persuade students to vote for green actions.
options.feedback: Correct! To persuade students to vote for green actions is right because Vote for a cleaner school directly asks readers to support the campaign.

options.text: To describe the landscape of a wide river.
options.feedback: The option about describing a river is wrong because no river landscape is painted and the text pushes action rather than description.

options.text: To inform students about final exam dates.
options.feedback: The option about informing of exam dates is wrong because no dates or subjects are announced and the focus is environmental votes.

options.text: To entertain readers with a cartoon adventure.
options.feedback: The option about entertaining with a cartoon is wrong because there is no funny story and the tone is serious campaign persuasion.

questions.explanation: Calls such as vote, join or act now signal persuasion. Descriptive passages lack that direct appeal and simply paint a scene for the reader.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Text: Teenagers need sleep, healthy food and sport. A balanced routine improves mood and marks. Which sentence best summarises the main idea?
questions.context: Marco is learning to find the sentence that best summarises.

options.text: A balanced daily routine keeps teenagers healthy.
options.feedback: Correct! A balanced daily routine keeps teenagers healthy is the best summary because sleep, food and sport together express the full message.

options.text: Eating carrots on Monday is the only healthy habit.
options.feedback: The sentence about carrots on Monday is wrong because one vegetable on one day is a narrow detail and not the whole routine.

options.text: The football coach shouts loudly during training.
options.feedback: The sentence about a football coach shouting is wrong because the coach never appears and shouting is unrelated to the healthy habits theme.

options.text: Buying a red bicycle makes everyone very happy.
options.feedback: The sentence about buying a red bicycle is wrong because no purchase is discussed and a bicycle alone cannot summarise the routine.

questions.explanation: Summarising means keeping the overall habit and result. Single foods or single days are details that support but do not equal the healthy routine.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Paragraph: Rain forms when water evaporates, rises, cools and falls from clouds. This cycle repeats every day. What is the purpose?
questions.context: Sara is identifying explanatory texts in her coursebook.

options.text: To explain how rain forms and falls.
options.feedback: Correct! To explain how rain forms and falls is right because the paragraph describes evaporation and clouds as a causal process.

options.text: To entertain with a tale about brave dragons.
options.feedback: The option about entertaining with dragons is wrong because no fantasy creatures appear and the tone is factual rather than playful.

options.text: To persuade readers to visit a new museum.
options.feedback: The option about persuading a reader to visit a museum is wrong because the passage makes no recommendation and no persuasive appeal appears in the text, so the author's purpose cannot be to invite anyone to go.

options.text: To inform passengers about current bus delays.
options.feedback: The option about informing of bus delays is wrong because no transport news is given and the focus is a natural water cycle.

questions.explanation: Explanatory writing answers how or why with steps and causes. Stories about dragons aim to amuse, while invitations aim to persuade, not explain.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report: Twenty volunteers cleaned the city river on Sunday. They removed plastic and cans. The water looks clear now. Choose the best title.
questions.context: Pablo is judging which title captures the main idea best.

options.text: Volunteers Clean the City River.
options.feedback: Correct! Volunteers Clean the City River is the best title because it names both the actors and the central cleaning action of the report.

options.text: Ducks Swim Happily in Spring.
options.feedback: The title about ducks in spring is wrong because ducks are only a background detail and cannot represent the volunteer cleaning effort.

options.text: A School Trip to London.
options.feedback: The title about a trip to London is wrong because no travel to London occurs and the river event is entirely local.

options.text: How to Buy Plastic Bottles.
options.feedback: The title about buying plastic bottles is wrong because the report opposes plastic waste and never recommends buying more bottles.

questions.explanation: A strong title names the topic plus the main point. Titles that mention only one detail or an unrelated trip mislead the reader about content.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Column: Cycling is the best way to move. It is cheap, clean and fast. Everyone should choose a bike. What is the purpose?
questions.context: Elena is analysing purpose clues in opinion columns.

options.text: To persuade readers that cycling is the best option.
options.feedback: Correct! To persuade readers that cycling is best is right because should choose and cleaner make a clear evaluative recommendation to act.

options.text: To give neutral news about traffic in the city.
options.feedback: The option about neutral news on traffic is wrong because evaluative words like best and should choose go beyond neutral reporting.

options.text: To entertain readers with an exciting bike race.
options.feedback: The option about entertaining with a race is wrong because no exciting race story is told and the style is argumentative.

options.text: To explain in detail how to repair a bicycle.
options.feedback: The option about explaining bike repair is wrong because no tools or repair steps are listed and the focus is opinion, not instructions.

questions.explanation: Opinion writers persuade by giving views and reasons plus a recommendation. Pure news reports avoid evaluative adjectives and direct recommendations.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Biography: Born poor, she studied hard, became a doctor and created cheap vaccines. What is the main idea?
questions.context: Diego is practising with short biographies of famous people.

options.text: A scientist overcame hardship to help medicine.
options.feedback: Correct! A scientist overcame hardship to help medicine is the main idea because poverty, study and vaccines together show a life achievement.

options.text: She won exactly one prize in the month of June.
options.feedback: The sentence about winning one prize in June is wrong because a single award is a detail within a much wider life story.

options.text: She liked chocolate cake for her birthday party.
options.feedback: The sentence about liking chocolate cake is wrong because food preferences are irrelevant and never mentioned in the biography.

options.text: Her school football team lost every single match.
options.feedback: The sentence about a school football team is wrong because sport is not discussed and cannot summarise a medical research career.

questions.explanation: Biographies inform by presenting life facts in order. The main idea covers the whole achievement, while one prize or school is only a part.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Debate text: Some say homework helps memory. Others say it causes stress. Both views deserve attention. What is the purpose?
questions.context: Carmen is evaluating author intent in two sided debates.

options.text: To inform readers about homework pros and cons.
options.feedback: Correct! To inform readers about homework pros and cons is right because the text gives both sides in neutral language for reflection.

options.text: To persuade readers to ban all homework forever.
options.feedback: The option about persuading to ban homework is wrong because the text keeps both views and never demands a ban as the only solution.

options.text: To entertain readers with jokes about school life.
options.feedback: The option about entertaining with school jokes is wrong because no humour is used and the style stays factual and balanced.

options.text: To describe the new canteen menu in detail.
options.feedback: The option about describing a canteen menu is wrong because food is never mentioned and the topic is homework arguments.

questions.explanation: Balanced debates inform by showing pros and cons. One sided slogans persuade, while jokes entertain, so neutral presentation signals information.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Passage: The village has stone houses, narrow streets and slow evenings. Smoke rises over the hills. What is the purpose?
questions.context: Andres is distinguishing descriptive purpose from persuasion.

options.text: To describe a quiet mountain village.
options.feedback: Correct! To describe a quiet mountain village is right because stone houses and slow evenings paint sensory images without any call to action.

options.text: To persuade readers to buy a new flat.
options.feedback: The option about persuading to buy a flat is wrong because no sale or price is offered and the tone is observational, not commercial.

options.text: To explain a difficult maths formula clearly.
options.feedback: The option about explaining a maths formula is wrong because no calculation or rule is presented and the focus is visual atmosphere.

options.text: To inform passengers about flight delays today.
options.feedback: The option about informing of flight delays is wrong because no travel news appears and the village portrait has no timetable.

questions.explanation: Descriptive purpose paints how something looks, sounds or feels. It uses sensory adjectives without urging the reader to buy, vote or join.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Paragraph: Take short showers. Turn off taps. Wash clothes with full loads. Choose the best heading.
questions.context: Lucia is choosing headings that match paragraph main ideas.

options.text: Simple Ways to Save Water at Home.
options.feedback: Correct! Simple Ways to Save Water at Home is the best heading because short showers and full loads express the whole saving idea.

options.text: How Taps Are Made in a Factory.
options.feedback: The heading about a tap factory is wrong because manufacturing taps is never discussed and narrows the home habits theme.

options.text: Results of a Swimming Contest.
options.feedback: The heading about a swimming contest is wrong because no contest is reported and sport misses the conservation message.

options.text: The Long History of Pipes.
options.feedback: The heading about the history of pipes is wrong because history is not explained and the paragraph focuses on present actions.

questions.explanation: Headings must reflect the main idea, not a detail. A paragraph about water saving needs a heading about saving water, not about one tap model.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Notice: Exams start on June tenth. Silence is required. Bring identity cards. No phones allowed. What is the purpose?
questions.context: Marco is detecting irony free purpose in formal notices.

options.text: To inform students of exam rules and dates.
options.feedback: Correct! To inform students of exam rules is right because silence and dates give binding instructions in a formal neutral register.

options.text: To entertain readers with funny exam anecdotes.
options.feedback: The option about entertaining with exam anecdotes is wrong because no funny stories are told and the register stays official.

options.text: To persuade students to buy expensive pens.
options.feedback: The option about persuading to buy pens is wrong because no product is sold and the notice only sets conduct rules.

options.text: To describe a lively party in the library.
options.feedback: The option about describing a library party is wrong because no celebration is announced and the content is purely regulatory.

questions.explanation: Formal notices inform and request compliance with rules. They use polite directives and dates, not humour or sales patter, to guide behaviour.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Argument: Night buses help young workers return safely. They reduce cars and keep streets lively. What is the main idea?
questions.context: Sara is judging main idea in longer argumentative paragraphs.

options.text: Night buses improve safety and nightlife access.
options.feedback: Correct! Night buses improve safety and nightlife access is the main idea because safer streets and late jobs give the full argument for the service.

options.text: One friendly driver is called Luis and smiles.
options.feedback: The sentence about one driver named Luis is wrong because a single driver is anecdotal evidence and cannot carry the whole policy argument.

options.text: Ticket machines sometimes freeze in cold winter.
options.feedback: The sentence about ticket machines in winter is wrong because machines are a minor operational detail unrelated to the safety claim.

options.text: Owls sleep quietly during the cold night hours.
options.feedback: The sentence about owls sleeping at night is wrong because owls are irrelevant to urban transport and add no argumentative support.

questions.explanation: Argumentative main ideas state a position plus a reason. Examples of one neighbour or one night are evidence, not the claim the author defends.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Leaflet: Our square was built in nineteen hundred. Litter harms birds. Join us on Saturday to clean it! What is the main purpose?
questions.context: Pablo is tackling advanced purpose questions with mixed tones.

options.text: To persuade neighbours to join clean up days.
options.feedback: Correct! To persuade neighbours to join clean up days is right because Join us on Saturday turns prior facts into a direct appeal for action.

options.text: To give a neutral history of the old square.
options.feedback: The option about neutral history of the square is wrong because the final call to join goes beyond neutral history into active persuasion.

options.text: To entertain children with tales of ghosts.
options.feedback: The option about entertaining with ghost tales is wrong because no ghost story is told and the tone is civic rather than spooky.

options.text: To explain the system of parking fines clearly.
options.feedback: The option about explaining parking fines is wrong because no fines or rules are detailed and the focus is community participation.

questions.explanation: Mixed texts blend information with gentle persuasion. The closing call to volunteer reveals persuasion as the dominant purpose beyond neutral facts.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Story: Two teams made posters. One planned early and finished calmly. The other started late and failed. What is the implied main idea?
questions.context: Elena is facing the hardest inference of implied main idea.

options.text: Preparation decides success in school projects.
options.feedback: Correct! Preparation decides success in school projects is the implied idea because ready teams finishing calmly points to that general lesson.

options.text: Buying blue folders guarantees excellent school marks.
options.feedback: The sentence about buying blue folders is wrong because folders are a superficial detail and never linked to project success in the story.

options.text: Rain often cancels football matches in spring.
options.feedback: The sentence about rain cancelling matches is wrong because weather is absent from the text and cannot explain the project contrast.

options.text: Teachers enjoy long coffee breaks every morning.
options.feedback: The sentence about teachers liking coffee breaks is wrong because teacher habits are irrelevant and miss the preparation theme entirely.

questions.explanation: Implied main ideas are never stated word for word. You must infer the general lesson about preparation from repeated contrasts between ready and unready teams.
questions.subject: ingles
